title: A Grand Entrance for the Grocery Run
angle: Automatic doors give ordinary errands a momentary theatrical entrance, then close before anyone can mistake the welcome for a personal endorsement.
paragraphs: Automatic doors are generous with their attention. Approach with a shopping cart, a reusable bag, or nothing but a vague intention to look at the bakery, and they swing open as if the building has been expecting you. For half a second, even a routine errand gets the treatment of an arrival.

The ceremony is wonderfully indiscriminate. The doors cannot distinguish a person with a carefully planned list from someone who has forgotten why they came in. They welcome both with equal confidence, then shut promptly behind them. No lingering welcome, no questions about whether the trip is going well. Just a brief flourish and the produce section.

There is something reassuring about a piece of machinery that offers a little drama without demanding that you earn it. A supermarket entrance does not care whether you are impressive, prepared, or wearing shoes that make sense for the weather. It opens because you are there. Then it gets on with its day, which is more than can be said for some hosts.

Maybe that is the ideal scale of recognition: a small courtesy, freely given, with no expectation that the moment become meaningful. The doors part; the cart rolls through; someone stops to check a text just inside the entrance. The grand entrance has its limits, and apparently one of them is foot traffic.
